speaker: CHIEF JUSTICE
text: This is here on a petition for further review.

speaker: CHIEF JUSTICE
text: Mr. Wakeman, is that correct?

speaker: CHIEF JUSTICE
text: All right, thank you. And Mr. Mossman, do either of you have any questions before we proceed?

speaker: CHIEF JUSTICE
text: Very good. Mr. Wakeman, then you may proceed.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: Good morning. May it please the Court. I'm E .M .R. Wakeman on behalf of the Appellants here, the Court Myers.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: Today we're asking this Court to reverse the Court of Appeals order and grant the Court Myers' request a quiet title. This is a case stemming from a claim for adverse possession.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: Our assignment is enumerated by five errors, but just like the elements for adverse possession, many of them do overlap, and there's a lot of nuance involved.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: Some of the factual background here is the Appellants are the owners of a parcel of real property currently known as Lot 27. It was previously referred to as Lot 30, and you would see that in Exhibit 44, which is a focal point of the primary emphasis of dispute.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: And the Appellee's or their entities are owners of Lot 26.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: The Appellants, they purchased their lot in 1990, and the Appellee's purchased their lot in around 2018, 2019.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: And the contention that the Court Myers are making is that they've adversely possessed a portion of Lot 26, which extends from their boundary line west 7 .2 feet.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: And I would assert that that adverse possession began first in 1990 and continued through the time of the trial in 2021.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: However, one of the main points of dispute here is that the Court Myers did nothing more than mere maintenance for many of those years. I would, of course, dispute that. They did maintain the property. That's undisputed. But they also planted trees on the disputed property. They stored various vehicles and pieces of equipment, and they did, of course, mow it.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: And then they also just planted many different plants and other items there. Now, the real significant improvements were done in about the fall of 2003 or early 2004. The record's a little bit blurry, but there's a lot of evidence submitted showing that they did, in fact, install a pretty significant retaining wall. And there was some different, I forget the term for it, but various structures that plants and vines would grow up on. Prior to that point, prior to 2003 -ish, can you point us to any cases that suggest routine maintenance, mowing, trimming, et cetera, constitutes adverse possession?

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: Justice, I do think that it's fair to say that you need something more than routine maintenance generally.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: Obviously, that analysis is mostly in line with the notoriousness of the adverse possession and that you need to put the actual owner on notice that you're laying claim to their piece of property. But I think the facts here can be distinguished in that not only the Kortmeyers and the Apolles, but also their predecessors and interests, the evidence would show that all of those parties believe that the Kortmeyers did, in fact, own this piece of property. So I think in light of that, the notorious element would be met in viewing it like that because the actual owner did, in fact, believe that the Kortmeyers owned it. And so they must have been doing enough to show that.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: And I would also submit to the court... If it's a mistaken fact, is it open and notorious?

speaker: JUSTICE (NEBRASKA SUPREME COURT)
text: If they thought they owned that, how is that open and notorious?

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: Yes, Justice, there is case law and...

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: Metinbrink and also Petch v. Widger. It's a 1997 case and the latter is a 1983 case. It's that the intent satisfies the hostile or adverse requirement, and an adverse possessor can succeed in his claim even if he or she doesn't know that they're actually adversely possessing the piece of disputed property.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: It is a bit nuanced, I would agree.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: However, if all of the parties believe that they owned it, I mean, hasn't there been sufficient notice?

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: That would be what I would posit to the court.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: Of course, most of this argument lies before the time period beginning in 2003 or early 2004 with the significant improvements. Mr. Waichman, there was a period of time where your clients began paying rent with Lot 26.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: When did that happen? So I would generally dispute that they've ever paid rent in the true sense of the word to use the quote from the Court of Appeals in Exhibit 44.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: I think what the Court of Appeals has said is that they have actually ordered that they pay a sum for services.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: And so what is very nuanced and interesting about that is the court mayers own the lot and the trailer on Lot 27. But on Lot 26, they only own the trailer, not the lot. Now, they pay the same sum for both parcels, if you will. And so there's not any consideration assigned to the actual lease of any property. The trial court seemed to hold on to that evidence, suggesting that you cannot take property from a landlord.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: They did, and I would assign error to that, Justice. In what way? Well, I think first off, the contract that Exhibit 44 shows, it was a contract implied at law, so it required a meeting of minds. And if the court mayers and the predecessor of interest had a meeting of minds, but neither party thought that the predecessor of interest owned the disputed property, well, then how could the court mayers have actually leased it, even if you assume that they are paying some sum or that there's a leasehood involved?

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: I would, of course, dispute that there is a lease involved at all and that they were just paying for mere services, especially since there's not consideration assigned to it. But especially when you view it in light of the fact that there needs to be a meeting of the minds, how could there be that if both parties thought that the court mayers owned that disputed property? Did the Court of Appeals discussion about Lot 26 and the fees that the court mayers were paying for Lot 26 being for utilities develop from evidence in this case, or was that based on the 2013 case?

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: Justice, when you're referring to the Court of Appeals, are you referring to the lower court in this case? Yes. I'm asking that question.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: I would say that they're primarily referring to evidence in this case by way of Exhibit 44, but they're taking the language from that order in order to make their ruling on this case. The order you're referring to is the 2013 case? That's correct. And that's the order that specifies that the court mayers were ordered to pay for services from 2009 and thereafter.

speaker: MR. WAKEMAN
text: For Lot 26. For Lot 26.
